citation: Sutfin N; Rowland J (2019): Depth and elevation of floodplain fine sediment along the East River near Crested Butte, Colorado measured in 2016 and 2017. Incorporating the Hydrological Controls on Carbon Cycling in Floodplain Ecosystems into Earth System Models (ESMs). Dataset. doi:10.15485/1574502

dataset.name: Depth and elevation of floodplain fine sediment along the East River near Crested Butte, Colorado measured in 2016 and 2017
description: The depth of floodplain fine sediment was measured at 1,601 points along the East River near Crested Butte, Colorado spanning a study reach approximately 800 m in length in 2016 and 2017. These depths are being used to estimate the volume of floodplain sediment present along the study reach, converted into mass of sediment using bulk density measurements, and finally used to estimate the mass of organic carbon stored in the floodplain based on elemental analysis of percent organic carbon content. Recorded depths include a minimum of 1 cm, a median of 56 cm, a maximum of 175 cm, and a mean with standard deviation of 61 ± 34 cm. This data include a csv file of the coordinates for each point in NAD 83 UTM zone 13, measured sediment depths, distance from the river channel active during 2015 measured using geographic information systems, the elevation of the floodplain surface derived from 0.5-m resolution lidar, and the elevation of the underlying gravel/bedrock surface, and in some cases the distance from the active channel measured in the field along the sampling transect. Also included is an ESRI ArcMap shapefile of the measurement points complete with the data listed above.

measurementTechnique: Depths of fine sediment (< 2mm in diameter) were recorded by inserting a soil probe approximately 1.27 cm in diameter and 180 cm in length vertically into the floodplain surface until refusal at bedrock or sediment larger than ~2 mm in diameter (i.e., pebbles/cobbles). Measurements were taken along transects orthogonal to the river channel in some location and sporadically through the study reach with special attention given to valley edges and river banks. Additional points are included with depths equal to zero located in the active river channel and along point bars composed of gravel and/or sand. The elevation of the underlying gravel surface was estimated as the elevation of the surface topography extracted from 0.5-m resolution aerial lidar minus the measured depth of floodplain fine sediment. Depth measurement locations were surveyed using a Trimble differential global positioning system, R10 rover, and R10 base station to provide a post-processing accuracy within 1 cm. The elevation of the ground surface at each measurement location was determined based on its location on the 2015 aerial lidar DEM with 0.5 meter resolution.
